paragraphs: Deutsche Telekom CEO Tim Höttges said on an earnings call on Thursday that he takes SpaceX seriously but doubts it can make Starlink Mobile a major US carrier without spending at least $200 billion, according to The Verge. Deutsche Telekom is the parent company of T-Mobile.

Höttges laid out his math. He said SpaceX has bought 76 megahertz of spectrum, while his company holds 400. Building a comparable spectrum position, he said, would take "triple-digit billions." He added that Musk could rent towers, but that building a network would still require another $20 billion to $30 billion. "If he has the money, go for it," he said, adding, "welcome to the party."

The Verge reports that SpaceX laid out its plans last month for Starlink Mobile to compete with T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon, using a mix of direct-to-cell satellites and a terrestrial network. It cites one recent report that SpaceX could tap into 80,000 US cell towers, and another that Musk was in talks to acquire Boost Mobile. The Verge also says Qualcomm announced this week that SpaceX will use its cellular infrastructure technology to support the network buildout.

Höttges also acknowledged a possible threat. He said Musk has chipsets, data centers, AI and satellites, and may integrate social media or agent models into the service, creating "a new way of communication services." He compared the situation to the car industry, which he said ignored a new competitor for too long. "But it's not a free lunch," he said, pointing to Tesla as an example.
The $200 billion figure is Höttges's own assessment as the head of a rival company. SpaceX's response was not included in the page text.

CesiumAstro announced that it has closed a $730 million Series D financing that values the company at more than $4.5 billion, according to the announcement published by SpaceNews. The round brings the company's total capital announced in 2026 to more than $1.2 billion. Janus Henderson led the equity round, with participation from investors including Insight Partners, Sands Capital, Sumitomo Corporation of Americas and Woven Capital, Toyota's growth fund. The company also received $100 million in debt financing provided through the Export-Import Bank of the United States and JPMorgan.

The company also unveiled Synchronicity, a planned 737-satellite constellation for commercial, sovereign and defense missions. It follows the launch of CesiumAstro's first satellite, Element-1, which has begun on-orbit operations. The company says the constellation will support Ku-, Ka- and V-band communications, edge computing and multi-orbit operations, with AI used to optimize the network and allocate resources.

CesiumAstro says Synchronicity will draw on its vertically integrated technology, including custom silicon, active phased arrays, software-defined payloads, spacecraft and terminals. Founder and CEO Shey Sabripour said the company designed these elements "as one system." The announcement says the move takes the company beyond supplying space technology to operating its own infrastructure.

The company said it has made three acquisitions in the past 12 months: Jariet Technologies, a millimeter-wave semiconductor company; 1Aardvark, which works on mission software for national defense programs; and Vidrovr. It also announced a $500 million investment over five years to expand its Austin-area headquarters, including the purchase of 270,000 square feet of manufacturing space.

The new money will go toward technology development, US manufacturing capacity, next-generation spacecraft, Synchronicity deployment and international growth. These are the company's own statements; the page text does not say when the constellation would launch.

Salon, one of the early internet's pioneering publications, announced on Thursday that it is ceasing publication after 31 years. The closure comes weeks before its anniversary on November 20, according to The Guardian.

In an unsigned statement, Salon said that "the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years" and that its publishing model is "no longer sustainable." The Verge notes that Salon did not go into detail about why, though it says many websites are grappling with "Google Zero" and the impact of AI tools. Salon general manager Amanda Wolfe pointed The Verge to the announcement post when asked for comment.

Salon was founded in San Francisco in 1995 and later moved most of its editorial staff to New York City in the 2000s. It built its reputation on politics, arts and culture coverage. The Guardian reports that a 2011 Columbia Journalism Review piece described it as the oldest general interest publication on the internet. It won Time magazine's website of the year for 1996 and BusinessWeek's best website for 1997.

In its statement, Salon said its work helped pioneer a form of journalism that would define a new era of publishing, and thanked the journalists, editors, photographers and others who made it. "What matters most is what happened during those years," it said.

The Verge reports that Find.co, which describes itself as a performance marketing ecosystem focused on crypto marketing, acquired Salon in 2023. Chief content officer Erin Keane said on Bluesky that the editorial archive will "stay live for now." The page text does not say what will happen to staff or the archive over the longer term.

Kalshi lost a series of federal court fights this week over whether state gambling laws apply to its prediction market, according to Ars Technica. Two federal appeals courts rejected its latest attempts to block enforcement in Connecticut, New York and Nevada, and Arkansas filed a new lawsuit against the company.

The core dispute is whether Kalshi's products are "swaps" that only the Commodity Futures Trading Commission can regulate, as Kalshi claims, or wagers that states can regulate. The full Ninth Circuit declined to rehear a ruling that let Nevada stop sports bets on Kalshi; no judge requested a vote. On Tuesday, a Second Circuit panel upheld lower-court decisions denying Kalshi preliminary injunctions against New York and Connecticut, finding it had not made the required showing. In September, the Sixth Circuit ruled that Ohio and Tennessee can enforce their gambling laws against Kalshi.

Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin filed his suit in state court. He said Kalshi "insists that its products are not gambling," but that "Arkansas law is concerned with substance, not semantics." He alleged that Kalshi offered wagering to people as young as 18 and did not pay taxes or comply with other restrictions. Ars Technica says it contacted Kalshi for comment and would update if it responded; no response was included. Utah's attorney general separately filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders about a week earlier.

The Trump administration is on Kalshi's side. The CFTC, which claims sole authority over such platforms, has sued ten states. Kalshi's biggest win came in April, when the Third Circuit held that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. New Jersey has asked the Supreme Court to reverse that ruling, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting its petition.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress on Thursday to approve at least $350 billion in defense funding while rejecting efforts to impeach him, according to Fox News. In a video posted to X, he called for a reconciliation bill to strengthen the military and the defense industrial base. "We need every vote from every patriotic member of Congress," he said.

Fox reports that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced eight articles of impeachment in September. They accuse Hegseth of violating congressional war powers during the Iran conflict and abusing his authority in other military operations. Massie lost his primary in May and plans to renew the effort when Congress returns next week. The House has not voted on the articles. Hegseth called them "sham articles" from "a disgruntled, defeated congressman" and his Democratic allies, and described the push as political theater. President Trump told ABC News he intends to keep Hegseth in his Cabinet. Massie's response to Hegseth's remarks was not in the page text.

Breaking Defense describes a tight calendar. Republicans have only five legislative weeks left in the year and are weighing a last attempt at party-line funding before Democrats take both chambers in January. The Pentagon has asked for a $1.15 trillion discretionary budget, the $350 billion mandatory request through reconciliation, and a supplemental request that includes $67 billion to recoup Iran war costs. Congress has approved none of them.

Analysts quoted by the outlet are skeptical. Todd Harrison of the American Enterprise Institute said the most likely outcome is that reconciliation does not even get a vote. Capital Alpha Partners' Byron Callan cut his odds of passage from 15 percent to 10 percent and put the chance of a government shutdown at 50 percent after the current stopgap funding expires Dec. 11. The House passed a budget resolution in July with $60 billion for defense, but Senate Majority Leader John Thune declined to bring it up, saying Republicans lacked the votes.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will headline the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention next week, the Washington Examiner reported. It will be his first speech since the midterm elections. He is scheduled to speak at 5 p.m. on Nov. 15 at the three-day convention in Washington, which is already sold out. His eldest daughter, Daniella, a student at the University of Virginia School of Law, will introduce him.

The announcement came Thursday as rumors of a possible resignation circulated after reports from the Independent and Bloomberg. Rubio denied them in an interview with the New York Times, saying it has "always been my plan" to finish his term. "I don't know where these things come from, to be honest with you," he told the paper.

Dylan Johnson, the assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, also rejected both stories on X. He called the Independent report "completely baseless fake news from made-up anonymous 'sources'" and wrote of the Bloomberg story, "Fake news. Totally made up." The page text does not say what the Independent or Bloomberg reports contained, and it does not include a response from either outlet.

The Examiner notes that the appearance comes as Democrats have told Republicans to "lawyer up" before both chambers of Congress shift to Democratic control. It says Democrats will win at least 54 Senate seats and 256 House seats and will take over in January 2027.

Speculation is also building over whether Rubio might run for president in 2028. He has previously said he has no plans to seek the White House, and he told the Times on Thursday, "I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore." Besides leading the State Department, Rubio serves as the president's national security adviser.

The Make America Healthy Again movement, centered on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., took a hit in Tuesday's midterms, according to Ars Technica. The outlet reports that many MAHA-favored candidates and allies lost while vocal critics of Kennedy won. It adds that the coalition was already strained, with supporters accusing Kennedy and the Trump administration of inaction and betrayals over two years in power.

Ars Technica describes MAHA as a loose coalition. A Politico poll in June found that people who identified with it held differing views on its priorities and had different political leanings. Some members embrace Kennedy's more fringe positions, which the outlet characterizes as false or unsupported, including a ban on water fluoridation and on mRNA vaccines. Others are drawn to goals such as better food quality, less exposure to environmental contaminants and less industry influence over health policy.

Discontent has grown. Some activists are angry that Kennedy has not banned mRNA vaccines. In February he drew backlash by backing Trump's push to increase domestic production of the pesticide glyphosate. In September he appeared at a MAHA-branded summit with large corporate sponsors, which prompted a critical response from former ally Robert Malone.

In October, Tiffany Cianci, a former supporter, published a scorecard listing 42 promises. It counts 37 broken, five partly fulfilled and none kept. Also in October, Kennedy adviser Calley Means resigned, reportedly disillusioned over delays in food policy changes. Influencer Vani Hari posted on election night: "Women don't come out to vote for glyphosate and war."

After the vote, activist Mary Talley Bowden polled followers on whether to start a third party, join the Democrats or overthrow the GOP. Joining the Democrats had about 3 percent at publication time, and a third party led narrowly.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases its October nonfarm payrolls report Friday at 8:30 a.m. ET. According to CNBC, economists surveyed by Dow Jones expect a gain of just 59,000 jobs, a slight rise from 29,000 in September. They expect the unemployment rate to hold at 4.2%.

CNBC reports that employers are reluctant to hire but are also not cutting staff. Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter, said the economy needs fewer new jobs to keep employment stable because fewer people are available to work. She pointed to retirements of an aging workforce, decades of low birth rates and a significant drop in immigration. She added that the economy is unlikely to return to gains of 200,000 or more a month.

The data show a slow stretch. From January 2025 through September 2026, payroll growth averaged 35,000 a month. Only one month topped 200,000, and seven months had losses. The unemployment rate rose just 0.2 percentage point over that period, while the labor force shrank by 434,000. The participation rate fell 0.8 percentage point to 61.8%.

Other measures look firmer. Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 last week, the lowest since July. Job openings rose by 333,000 in September. The number of workers quitting reached 3.36 million, its highest in a year and a half.

Long-term unemployment is a weak spot. The number of people out of work for more than 25 weeks is up by 495,000 since January 2025, and average unemployment duration is 24.8 weeks. Bachaud said it is hard for jobless people to break back in when turnover is low. CNBC says Federal Reserve officials generally view the labor market as solid, though questions remain.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government unveiled its second federal budget on Thursday, using an oil revenue windfall to fund tens of billions of dollars in new spending, the BBC reports. Titled Masters of Our Destiny, it focuses on national sovereignty and the high cost of living. "It's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said.

The BBC says the C$142 billion in new spending over five years is possible because of better-than-expected revenues from oil prices lifted by the Iran War. The deficit is over C$50 billion, with no path to balance, though the budget keeps Carney's earlier fiscal goals intact.

One of the largest items is C$11.2 billion over four years to combat homelessness, covering supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment. The budget also increases a grocery benefit, estimated at C$2,570 for a family of four. The BBC notes the Conservative opposition has pressed the Liberal government on cost of living and accused Carney of spending too much time on foreign trade missions. It also says wages have not kept pace with inflation and food bank use is at record highs.

On trade, the budget builds on efforts to reduce reliance on the United States and to cushion the effect of US tariffs. It supports sectors such as steel and forestry. The BC Council of Forest Industries said the support "comes at a critical time for workers." The budget says nearly C$44 billion has been set aside since March 2025 for workers and businesses hit by tariffs.

Immigration levels stay flat. Permanent resident admissions remain at 380,000 a year until 2028. Sovereignty spending includes C$2.7 billion for space technology and launch infrastructure, and a tax exemption on income from original artistic works.

Early results from South Africa's municipal elections show the African National Congress with a sharply reduced share of the vote, Al Jazeera reports. After more than 60 percent of votes were counted, election commission data late Thursday put the ANC at about 32 percent. The Democratic Alliance was second at 25 percent. Former President Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party was third at 8.5 percent, below what opinion polls had suggested.

Turnout was estimated at 54.5 percent, with about 15.9 million of 29.2 million registered voters casting ballots. That compares with 46 percent in the pandemic-hit 2021 local elections. Final results are expected on Sunday.

The ANC has been South Africa's largest party since it led the country out of apartheid in 1994, though it tends to do worse in local contests than national ones. It won nearly 70 percent nationally in 2004, fell to 46 percent in the 2021 municipal elections, and took just over 40 percent in the 2024 national vote. That result forced it into a unity government with nine other parties, including the DA. Al Jazeera says the ANC, led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, has borne criticism over municipal mismanagement, including failing water supplies, power cuts and crumbling services. It has also faced corruption allegations and the loss of support to splinter parties.

Control of the eight major metropolitan municipalities is at stake. Projections from the state-funded Council for Scientific and Industrial Research put the DA at 56 percent in Cape Town, where its leader Geordin Hill-Lewis has declared victory, and at 34 percent in Johannesburg. MK was projected at 32 percent in Durban. Outright majorities look uncertain in several cities, which could mean another round of coalition talks.

A wave of hoax bomb threats against European airlines and airports has prompted diversions and, in Italy, an escort by fighter jets, the BBC reports. The threats targeted one airline or airport after another. Nearly all were treated as credible enough to divert the aircraft involved, with London's Heathrow a notable exception. All turned out to be false, which the BBC notes does not mean future threats will be.

The BBC says the simultaneous, coordinated nature of the hoaxes, along with other incidents in Europe, has led some people to suspect Russia. It lists earlier cyber-attacks, mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites, the remote hacking of supermarket freezers and a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and an August drone attack on Germany's Leipzig Halle airport that Germany's interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.

Some argue, on circumstantial evidence alone, that the hoaxes fit so-called hybrid or grey-zone warfare: anonymous, deniable actions that fall short of triggering NATO's Article 5. The BBC adds that Moscow is angry at NATO for supporting Ukraine, and that Russian bloggers have suggested Western countries should feel the same disruption Russian airports face from Ukrainian drones.

But as of Thursday evening, the BBC says, no hard evidence had linked the hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups. An email sent Thursday to Rome airport authorities was signed "Fighters of the Male State," a name that likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion, which a Moscow court banned in 2021. The BBC cautions that another group could be using the name, and that the email is unlikely to give investigators useful leads. It says police, airport authorities and transport ministries should follow concrete leads rather than assume the most likely culprits.

Police are investigating two further rape allegations against Russell Brand, and the lead detective has urged other possible victims to come forward, the Guardian reports. Brand, 51, was found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women over five years at the height of his career. He was cleared of two other rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court.

The Metropolitan police said Brand was interviewed under caution over two more rape allegations made by two women, and that files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service. Detectives remain in contact with prosecutors as inquiries continue. Brand also faces a civil claim in the UK from a woman who accuses him of sexually assaulting her at his Los Angeles mansion in 2008. In court papers seen by the Guardian, she alleges he forcibly removed her clothing and attempted a sex act against her will. The Guardian says he faces civil claims in Britain and the US. The page text does not include a response from Brand to these further allegations or claims.

Det Supt Andy Furphy called Brand "a predator" and said his behavior escalated as he became more famous. "We have a live investigation. Our work's not done," he said. He suggested the conviction could encourage others to come forward, and described it as a possible "watershed moment."

The Guardian says the investigation, Operation Actinolite, involved more than 100 witnesses, more than 1,400 documents and more than 340 statements. Furphy said Brand gave interviews and kept podcasting during the trial, which took a toll on the women. He said Brand "drove right up to the line of what was acceptable" but stopped short of it.

IREN, a company that sells AI computing capacity, said in its earnings report on Thursday that more than $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to land in 2026 has been pushed out to at least January. Payment could extend to February. CNBC reported that the company attributed the move to "a customer-requested change and supplier timing." On the earnings call, co-CEO Daniel Roberts said Microsoft is the customer. He said it asked to reconfigure and upgrade some network infrastructure to enable 200 megawatts of capacity for the latest-generation frontier models.

Quarterly revenue rose 66% from the prior quarter to $228 million, above the $221 million average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AI Cloud revenue more than doubled to $200 million, and the rest came from bitcoin mining. Net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million. Backlog rose 22% to $20.3 billion, with about two-thirds from investment-grade counterparties, the company said. It added that the $4 billion target is fully contracted and funded.

The report followed a 26% post-election drop in IREN's shares, and a 55% fall over the past month. Shares rose in extended trading. CNBC said investors are watching for signs of an AI-trade unwinding, with concern that debt-reliant companies may struggle as interest rates rise and lenders retreat. The Nasdaq had its worst day since April 2025. CoreWeave, down 60% in a month, reports Tuesday. Nebius, down 48%, reports next Thursday.

Roberts said capital markets have become more selective and the question has shifted to whether projects can be delivered, financed and run profitably. He also described a "disconnect" between public markets and customers. IREN plans $15 billion in capital spending the rest of this fiscal year: $9 billion in cash and committed financing, and $6 billion in target financing that is subject to market conditions. Roberts said one customer agreed to fund 90% of GPU capital spending. The company said it deliberately has not yet bought all the GPUs it needs for next year.

Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday that Democratic wins in the midterm elections will make it considerably harder for companies to build data centers. She said the industry has "not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments," according to TechCrunch. Data centers were very much on the ballot this season, and some politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms.

Powell McCormick tied the backlash to broader feelings about AI. "The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center," she said, and people can say they do not want one in their community. She said Meta hopes to improve sentiment by showing the value of both the facilities and the technology itself, and described Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg as "long human."

She said Meta has built data centers for 20 years and now has them in 23 states. Five, including one in Texas, are planned at 1 gigawatt or more. Building has been hard, she said, and "it's going to be harder," though it is becoming clear which models work and states want them.

She said communities want data centers only when they benefit. By her description, Meta's approach has it pay for its own electricity, direct any resulting tax surplus toward teachers and first responders, keep the labor force local and seek bipartisan support. She expects projects to face more review and to be weighed against whether constituents want them.

On the financial risk, Meta has pinned hopes on AI products, including its consumer agent Muse, which has 10 million users today. Powell McCormick said that even if that scale does not arrive, the compute will be valuable. "We're getting calls every day to lease that compute," she said, adding that Meta sees a path to monetization either way.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday that it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned group toward the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest cities, according to Al Jazeera. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said air defenses "intercepted and destroyed" the missile. The announcement came minutes after Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency warned of potential danger near the port of Yanbu. The agency later said the threat had passed.

The Houthis rejected the claim that they targeted Medina, calling it a "blatant and grave falsehood." Military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X that the group's operations "target only oil facilities and military bases." Al Jazeera noted that the Houthis have attacked airports, energy infrastructure and military sites, and have targeted Yanbu several times in recent months. Yanbu is a major oil export hub and an outlet for crude moving through the kingdom's East-West pipeline, which has helped Riyadh ship crude and fuel since the US-Israeli war on Iran began in February.

Separately, Yemen's internationally recognized government said its forces took the Sanamat area in Taiz governorate. Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said forces carried out 1,298 "targeting operations" in 24 hours and killed about 400 Houthi fighters. Al Jazeera could not independently verify those claims. Late last month, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5. The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll.

Yazeed al-Jeddawy of the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies told Al Jazeera the conflict appears to be heading toward a prolonged war of attrition, since the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power in 30 days. He said the war is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation involving Iran.

Half of the US Navy's Japan-based destroyers are supporting the war on Iran, according to Defense One. Five of the 10 destroyers homeported in Yokosuka, along with the carrier George Washington, are deployed to US Central Command's area. Navy officials have told the crews of at least some of those destroyers that they will not return home until 2027.

Defense One said this conflicts with administration strategy documents. The National Security Strategy, released less than a year ago, says the days of the Middle East dominating American foreign policy "are thankfully over," and the January National Defense Strategy named the homeland and deterring China as top priorities. The article says President Trump launched the Iran war about five weeks later. Operation Epic Fury officially concluded in June, but the Pentagon keeps a large force in the region.

Ralph Cossa of the Pacific Forum said the absence is a problem for credibility and for allies who plan months ahead for carrier visits. Katherine Kuzminski of the Center for a New American Security said the long deployments suggest operations are not aligning with the stated strategies, making it hard to determine requirements. Cossa said he does not believe China will attack Taiwan next year, despite reports that Xi Jinping told his military to be ready by 2027. But he said having a third of the operational fleet in the Middle East "sends the wrong signal."

US Pacific Command pushed back on the suggestion that it is scaling back China deterrence. A spokesperson said its commitment to Indo-Pacific security "remains steadfast" and pointed to the recent Keen Sword exercise, which included the Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group. Deputy commander Lt. Gen. George Rowell said last week that deterrence is the command's highest duty.

The Royal International Air Tattoo, one of the world's biggest annual air shows, is leaving RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, after four decades and will move permanently to MOD Boscombe Down in Wiltshire, organizers announced Wednesday, according to Defense News. The move comes more than a month after a suspected Iranian threat at the base.

Organizers canceled the 2026 show in late May after talks with the Royal Air Force and the US Air Force, citing "uncertainty" over access to Fairford given the base's role in the Iran war. The US Air Force housed a dozen B-1B Lancers there during Operation Epic Fury, using them to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

After the suspected plot against the base in late September, the US removed all bombers from Fairford and returned them to their home stations. British officials said there are "strong indications" that Iran was involved. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied the accusation on social media. Five men were initially arrested and released on bail, and two were rearrested and charged under the UK National Security Act.

Organizers did not cite the plot as the reason for the move. They described the relocation as essential for the show's long-term future. "The decision to move RIAT to Boscombe Down is about much more than a new location," RAF Charitable Trust Chief Executive Gavin Gager said, adding that it is about securing the show and the charitable impact it generates.

The show usually draws more than 150,000 spectators. Its first edition at Boscombe Down, a British military airfield used for aircraft testing and evaluation that hosts two air squadrons and six units, is scheduled for July 16 to 18.

Nithya Raman was elected mayor of Los Angeles, defeating incumbent Karen Bass, according to The Guardian. The Associated Press called the race on Thursday, with returns showing Raman at just over 52% to Bass's 48%. Raman, a progressive urban planner, has served on the city council since 2020.

Her campaign was once viewed as a long shot. She entered the race hours before the filing deadline and shortly after endorsing Bass. Both candidates are progressives, and the race became a bitter contest between different wings of the party. The Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, of which Raman was a longtime member, endorsed her, and its volunteers knocked on doors citywide. The Guardian said she was often compared with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Shortly before the election, the group's national leaders considered rescinding the chapter's support until Raman stated her position on the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, but a vote on that failed.

Bass had never lost an election. The Guardian said she faced low approval ratings, public frustration over homelessness, rising costs and housing affordability, and anti-establishment sentiment. It also noted a large budget shortfall and the effects of the Trump administration's deportation campaign. Spencer Pratt, a former reality TV star and registered Republican who lost his home in the Palisades fire, ran a prominent campaign, but Raman narrowly beat him in the primary.

Raman pitched herself as a candidate who could lower rents, improve streets, reduce homelessness and keep people safe. She praised Bass in a video statement. Bass said she had called Raman to congratulate her and committed to a smooth transition.

Two more Republican-held House seats went to Democrats, according to reports from Fox News and the Washington Examiner. Fox News reported that the Associated Press projected late Thursday that Cait Conley, a military veteran and former Biden administration aide, will defeat two-term Rep. Mike Lawler in New York's 17th District. Conley served as counterterrorism director on the White House National Security Council from 2021 to 2023, then as a senior adviser on election security at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The district sits north of New York City and was won by Kamala Harris in 2024. Fox rated it "lean Democrat," while the Cook Political Report called it a toss-up.

Fox said the race featured sharp disagreement on immigration enforcement and taxes. Lawler, who sought to balance support for President Trump with an independent image, was backed by the parents of Sheridan Gorman, a student killed in Chicago. He argued that sanctuary laws are dangerous and that Conley would do nothing to limit illegal immigration. Conley condemned the killing and said she opposes illegal immigration, but Fox reported she has not spoken out against sanctuary laws specifically.

In Arizona's 6th District, the Washington Examiner reported that Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza, a Democrat, beat Rep. Juan Ciscomani, 53% to 44.9%, per the AP. Ciscomani had won in 2022 by 1.5 points and in 2024 by 2.5, and the district favored Trump by 0.7% in 2024. Mendoza campaigned against tariffs, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and spending on Middle East wars. Ciscomani cited his bipartisan record and called her too "extremist," the paper said. Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson had endorsed him.
The supplied pages did not cover the other races named in the card summary.

A former Alaska Republican lawmaker told Fox News Digital that the FBI interviewed him after a man he believes was a Democratic operative tried to recruit him into the state's US Senate race. The claim is part of a widening controversy over a so-called "Decoy Dan Sullivan" ballot scheme. The ballot ultimately listed Democrat Mary Peltola, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, Republican Gerald Heikes and retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan. Fox noted that whether the similarly named candidate diverted votes or affected the outcome remains unproven.

The controversy follows the New York Times reporting on former Peltola campaign staff describing a reported effort to add other candidates named Dan Sullivan to the ballot. Fox said Peltola's campaign and Democrats backed such a scheme, citing that report. Fox said it asked the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, Peltola's campaign and Wingspan Strategies for comment. Wingspan is where Jerid Kurtz is named in congressional documents as a co-owner. No response was reported in the article.

Former state Rep. David Eastman said he met an operative in Wasilla in April who claimed to represent conservative donors seeking candidates. Eastman later identified him in a blog post as Kurtz. Eastman said that was not true, but that the man never mentioned either Sullivan or any plan to confuse voters. He also said he received "fake mailers" implying Decoy Dan was the only Sullivan in the race. Fox said the mailers omit Senator Sullivan.

Will Chamberlain, an attorney with the Article III Project, argued that a coordinated effort to deceive voters could violate a federal conspiracy-against-rights statute. He acknowledged that no identical case exists. House Oversight Chairman James Comer asked Kurtz to appear for an interview on November 6 and warned of compulsory process if he does not.

Voters in several states decided ballot measures on transgender issues and noncitizen voting on Tuesday, even as Democrats won control of Congress. The Washington Examiner reported that measures banning biological males from female school sports passed in Nebraska and Arizona. Similar measures in Colorado and Washington were leading but not yet called. Colorado's Proposition 135, which would prohibit certain surgeries on minors, was also ahead with about 52% of the vote.

STAT said the votes crossed party lines, and Colorado Democrats won most major offices. Critics called the measures "ballot candy" for Republicans. STAT noted that the NCAA has said no transgender athletes currently compete in women's leagues, and that research does not suggest an inherent edge. Chase Strangio of the ACLU said ballot measures are "a function of funding more than anything." Colorado's measures are statutory, so lawmakers can amend them, and the governor-elect said they need "a long, hard look."

Fox News reported that Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved measures clarifying citizenship requirements for voting in state and local elections, each with over 60% support. Federal law already bars noncitizens from voting in federal elections. Conservative advocates said the results show broad support for proof-of-citizenship rules. Measures failed in California and Arizona. The Fox piece quoted only Republican-aligned voices, and no Democratic response was included.

On other topics, STAT reported that four states voted on abortion and all preserved the legal status quo. Missouri voters rejected a bid to reverse abortion protections, and Massachusetts voters kept recreational marijuana legal.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has authorized National Guard troops in Washington, D.C., to use dozens of marked police cars, military vehicles and boats, according to Fox News Digital. Two Pentagon officials confirmed that Hegseth signed an Oct. 29 memo. A War Department official said the guidance allows up to 60 marked patrol cars, military tactical vehicles, up to 20 light towers and generators, and D.C. National Guard boats in support of federal and local law enforcement operations. Fox reported that the memo also covers Humvees. Politico first reported the authorization.

About 3,000 Guard troops are deployed in the capital as part of President Trump's crime crackdown, which the department calls the "Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful" mission. Fox said the memo follows Hegseth's decision last year to let Guard troops carry service-issued weapons when their mission requires it. In related coverage, Fox cited the FBI as touting 6,000 arrests and a 44% drop in homicides one year into the crackdown.

Local officials are pressing for the deployment to end. D.C. Councilmember Brooke Pinto, who chairs the council's public safety committee, held a hearing Thursday on the federal law enforcement and Guard presence. She said she is hopeful that partners at the state and congressional level can "push back and demand that this unnecessary, harmful and unlawful military presence be removed."

Pinto called on newly elected Democratic governors in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas to withdraw the combined 628 troops she said their states have sent to Washington. She also urged congressional Democrats to increase oversight of federal law enforcement operations in January, including requirements for identifying badges and body cameras. The article did not report a White House or Pentagon response to the hearing.
